extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of 18th-century British periodicals; literary scholars and general readers of annotated historical texts
extracted.subtask_description: An edited, annotated edition of Steele's Tatler containing original essay text plus editorial footnotes and commentary; used for literary-historical reading and analysis of early-18th-century periodical practice, style, and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tatler editorial scope and subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: “shall take anything that offers for the subject of my discourse. Thus, new persons, as well as new things, are to come under my consideration; as, when a toast, or a wit, is first pronounced such, you shall have the freshest advice of their preferment, with a description of the beauty's manner, and the wit's style; as also, in whose places they are advanced.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper will not confine itself to political news but will include any material that 'offers'—new people and new things, notices of social preferment, and descriptive sketches (beauties' manner, wits' style). Policy favors prompt, fresh reports and character sketches as part of its remit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tatler tone and permissible trespass
rubrics_metrics.description: “I shall always take the liberty to tell for news such things (let them have happened never so much before the time of writing) as have escaped public notice, or have been misrepresented to the world, provided that I am still within rules, and trespass not as a Tatler any further than in an incorrectness of style, and writing in an air of common speech.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted editorial liberties: publish overlooked or previously misrepresented items; acceptable 'trespass' is stylistic informality and use of common/conversational speech. Substantive rules/limits should be respected even when repurposing older material as 'news.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unjust offence
rubrics_metrics.description: “it is my design, to avoid saying anything, of any person, which ought justly to displease”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer intends to steer clear of remarks that would rightly offend individuals; combine entertaining variety with restraint so as to 'give entertainment for men of pleasure, without offence to those of business.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrait-painting: composition, expression, and costume as conveyors of character
rubrics_metrics.description: “Clarissa is, by that skilful hand, placed in a manner that looks artless, and innocent of the torments she gives; Chloe drawn with a liveliness that shows she is conscious, but not affected, of her perfections... nothing could be better imagined than the dress he has given her, of a straw hat and riband, to represent that sort of beauty which enters the heart with a certain familiarity...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good portraiture employs pose and expression to convey character (artlessness vs. conscious liveliness) and uses costume/detail (e.g., straw hat and ribbon) to signal a social type or the emotional effect the sitter is meant to produce in viewers. Design choices should support the intended psychological reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre (stage) should engage understanding, not only senses
rubrics_metrics.description: “the stage being an entertainment of the reason and all our faculties, this way of being pleased with the suspense of them for three hours together, and being given up to the shallow satisfaction of the eyes and ears only, seems to arise rather from the degeneracy of our understanding, than an improvement of our diversions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of spectacles/operas that appeal only to sight and sound: dramatic entertainments ought to engage reason and the full faculties. Productions relying chiefly on sensory spectacle (and on foreign-language performance that blocks comprehension) are judged as cultural decline rather than progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/pamphlet writing: clarity, liveliness, and temperate passion
rubrics_metrics.description: “The real causes of the decay of the interest of religion, are set forth in a clear and lively manner, without unseasonable passions; and the whole air of the book, as to the language, the sentiments, and the reasonings, show it was written by one whose virtue sits easy about him, and to whom vice is thoroughly contemptible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective religious advocacy: present causes clearly and vividly, avoid excess or 'unseasonable' passion, and use language/sentiment/reason that reflect measured virtue and good breeding rather than rant or sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic excellence: naturalness and original thought
rubrics_metrics.description: “All Milton's thoughts are wonderfully just and natural... But now I can't forgive this odious thing, this Dryden, who, in his 'State of Innocence,' has given my great-grand-mother Eve the same apprehension of annihilation... Yet the verses are very good.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise is due where poetic thought feels 'just and natural' and exhibits originality; imitation of memorable images across poets is subject to criticism—even if verses are technically good, copying or repeating a distinctive conceit can be censured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of epithets in epic poetry (fit and consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Virgil is more judicious than the other in the epithets he gives his hero. 'Homer's usual epithet... his indiscretion has been often rallied by the critics, for mentioning the nimbleness of foot in Achilles, though he describes him standing, sitting, lying down, fighting, eating, drinking... Virgil's common epithet to Æneas, is 'Pius' or 'Pater.' I have therefore considered what passage there is ... where either of these appellations would have been most improper, ... the poet has therefore wisely dropped them both for Dux Trojanus.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epithets should be chosen with regard to contextual appropriateness; avoid stock epithets that produce incongruity or burlesque when applied in circumstances that contradict the epithet's implication. Judicious omission or replacement (e.g., Dux Trojanus) can preserve dignity and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative selection for moral instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thus if anything that is said, even of old Anchises or Æneas, be set by me in a different light than has hitherto been hit upon, in order to inspire the love and admiration of worthy actions, you will, gentle reader, I hope, accept of it for intelligence you had not before.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial reinterpretation of classical or historical narratives is acceptable when done to illuminate and inspire admiration of virtuous actions; reframing may be used pedagogically to promote moral exemplars, provided the reader is informed of the intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of beauty and their social/effectual consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: “The beauty of Clarissa is soft, that of Chloe piercing... Clarissa looks languishing; Chloe, killing. Clarissa never fails of gaining admiration; Chloe, of moving desire... The force of their different beauties is seen also in the effects it makes on their lovers. The admirers of Chloe are eternally gay and well-pleased: those of Clarissa, melancholy and thoughtful.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish character-types of beauty by features, demeanor, and sociopsychological effects: some beauties invite contemplative admiration, others immediate desire and gaiety. Such distinctions can be used in social description, character portrayal, and portraiture to explain differing behavioral consequences among admirers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities leading to greatness/leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: “such elevations are the natural consequences of an exact prudence, a calm courage, a well-governed temper, a patient ambition, and an affable behaviour.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greatness is attributed to stable personal arts/virtues—prudence, measured courage, self-control, sustained ambition, and affability—rather than to chance. These are presented as both the means to rise and the pillars maintaining a leader's stature.
